problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,x>0.
$$
worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =-1 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-2+\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{-2-\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{-2+\text{i}}+B{x}^{-2-\text{i}} \\  & =A\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}+B\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=1$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{({c}_{2}-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-(1+2{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & ={c}_{2}-2 \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
